content: Is there a way to access an array element in unsafe code, without proving the index is valid, where the element type is not Inhabited? I'm using a[i]'lcProof to fake a proof that the index is valid, but I wonder if there is a better way to do this.

I don't think so. Unsafe or not it seems like there would still need to be some value level term that infers as the relevant type in order for the declaration to be valid.

Out of curiosity, what are you putting in an array that you can't determine is inhabited?

Chris Bailey said:

what are you putting in an array that you can't determine is inhabited?

Tactic.SavedState, which is clearly inhabited but cannot be proved due to Environment having a private constructor.
But you can non-constructively obtain an Inhabited from a Nonempty, and this will solve your problems!
surely this would make the code noncomputable, which defeats the purpose of writing it?

If you're in TermElabM or one of the other metaprogramming monads, it should be pretty easy to just do a check to see whether the access is in-bounds and use the monad's error handling to avoid this in the first place, I would think.

My initial thought was that you may be able to make an unsafe instance as such:

unsafe instance : GetElem (Array α) Nat α fun _ _ => True where
  getElem xs i _ := xs.getInternal i lcProof

unsafe example (arr : Array α) : α := arr[0] --works

But as it turns out, unsafe instances "leak" to the safe world and may be be synthesised in non-unsafe declarations, leading to a kernel error:

/-- error: (kernel) invalid declaration, it uses unsafe declaration 'instGetElemArrayNatTrue_foo' -/
#guard_msgs in
example (arr : Array α) : α := arr[0]

I would suggest adding a Array.unsafeGet function to the library implemented as a[i]'lcProof (not very sure if this is the correct use of lcProof, though)

Also I think Environment can be made Inhabited, and that would make many things easier.
unsafe instance is a bad idea since it obscures the use of unsafe code. Consider using a unsafe local instance so it doesn't leak to other modules.
Unsafe cannot be obscured - it spreads to anything that depends on it. But I agree that using unsafe code is a bad idea, unless there is absolutely no alternative.
